issues.issue: The notice says the Policy covers ONLY Claims first made during the Policy Period or Extended Reporting Period, while Section VI.A (Awareness Provision) deems Claims arising from a noticed Potential Claim to have been made in the earlier Policy Period. A court could be asked whether the caps notice restricts or is qualified by the deeming provisions in VI.A and V.A.

The declarations text is so garbled that the identity of the Parent Company and the assignment of the inception/expiration dates run together with the address block. A court could be asked what the Declarations actually designate under Item 1 and Item 2.
The stated aggregate limit reads "3 10,000,060", a figure that is on its face a mis-transcription of a round $10,000,000. A court could be asked what limit the Declarations actually fix.
The retention reads "3 256,000", an odd figure that appears to be a mis-transcription of $250,000. A court could be asked what per-Claim retention the Declarations set.

The Yes/No boxes are rendered as stray characters, so whether Punitive Damages Coverage is "Included" cannot be read off the face of Item 6. That election controls the final paragraph of the definition of Loss.

The Yes/No boxes are rendered as stray characters, so whether Third Party Claim Coverage is included cannot be determined from Item 7. Insuring Agreement B and the definition of Claim both turn on that election.

Item 8 declares that Terrorism Coverage was purchased with no separate premium, yet nothing in the policy form (Sections I through VIII) defines or grants terrorism coverage. A court could be asked what, if anything, Item 8 adds to the Insuring Agreements.

The clause says the Policy is not valid unless signed by "another duly authorized representative" in addition to the attesting officers, without identifying who qualifies. A court could be asked whether the countersignature requirement was met.

Insuring Agreement A reads "made against any Insured by or on behaif Employee", omitting words so that it is unclear whether the covered Claim must be brought by an Employee, on behalf of an Employee, or both. That omission goes to the core grant of coverage.

The reporting condition caps notice at sixty days after expiration of the Policy Period, while Section VI.C gives sixty days after the Claim is first made and Section VI.A deems earlier-noticed Potential Claims to be Claims. The two reporting deadlines can produce different outside dates for the same Claim.

The paragraph defines lower-case "spouse" to "include" domestic partners without saying whether the list is exhaustive, and the extension elsewhere speaks of a "lawful spouse". Whether a non-marital partner qualifies could be argued either way.

The right to an Extended Reporting Period arises only if the Insurer non-renews or the Parent Company cancels, yet Section VIII.C.2 allows the Insurer itself to cancel for nonpayment, a situation this clause does not address and the next paragraph appears to exclude. A court could be asked whether an ERP is available on an insurer cancellation.

The sixty-day election window runs from "the effective date of cancellation, or nonrenewal as appropriate", but nonrenewal has no stated effective date. A court could be asked when the clock starts on a nonrenewal.

This sentence limits ERP coverage to Claims first made during the ERP, while the very next sentence deems any such Claim to have been made during the immediately preceding Policy Period. The two deeming rules have to be reconciled with Insuring Agreement I's "first made" condition.

The deeming of ERP Claims into the preceding Policy Period sits against Section II.C's requirement that they be first made during the ERP and against Section V.A's limit for "Claims first made during the Policy Period". Which period a Claim belongs to could be litigated.

"Application" sweeps in "any other such documents submitted in connection with the underwriting" and any publicly available DOL/EEOC filings, a catch-all whose outer edge against the enumerated signed applications is undefined. Because the Application is made the basis of the Policy, its reach is consequential.

"Benefits" ends with the catch-all "any other payment to or for the benefit of an employee arising out of the employment relationship" while excluding salary, wages and commissions, leaving the boundary between the catch-all and the carve-out contestable. The line matters because Exclusion B.1 limits recovery of Benefits to Defense Costs.

"Claim" turns on "a written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief", an undefined phrase whose application to letters, charges and pre-suit correspondence is the classic claims-made battleground; the paragraph also speaks of an Insured "receiv[ing]" a civil proceeding. When a Claim was first made is the pivotal issue under this policy.

Defense Costs are limited to "reasonable and necessary" legal fees and expenses, a standard with no benchmark or determination mechanism in the Policy. Disputes over the reasonableness of fees turn on that phrase.

"Discrimination" is defined as violation of any statute, regulation, ordinance or common law "concerning discrimination in employment anywhere in the world", leaving the class of qualifying laws unbounded. Whether a given statutory theory is "concerning discrimination in employment" could be argued.

"Employee" includes leased persons, volunteers and independent contractors on terms that differ from the parallel list in III.J (Insured Individual), which requires a prior written indemnity agreement for the same categories. The overlap invites argument over who is covered as what.

The definition closes with "illegal work related harassment" after two specific sexual-harassment limbs, a general catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain. Whether non-sexual workplace conduct qualifies would turn on that third limb.

The categories of Insured Individual overlap but do not match the categories of "Employee" in III.G, notably for volunteers, leased persons and independent contractors. Which definition governs a particular claimant is left to be worked out.

"Interrelated Wrongful Acts" turns on a "common nexus" of "any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction, cause or series of causally or logically connected" facts, a formulation that is famously elastic and has no limiting principle. It drives both the prior-acts exclusion and the single-Claim rule.

"Loss" excludes "matters uninsurable under the law applicable to this Policy" without identifying the applicable law, while the punitive-damages paragraph adopts a most-favorable-jurisdiction rule; the two insurability standards sit uneasily together. Whether particular damages are Loss would turn on which standard applies.

Other Workplace Torts are covered "only when alleged as part of a Claim for" the enumerated wrongs, and the degree of connection required by "as part of" is undefined. A claimant pleading defamation alongside a discrimination count would test that limit.

"Policyholder" covers Parent plus Subsidiaries, yet operative clauses (e.g. VIII.C Cancellation and the Authorization Clause) give rights only to the Parent Company and Section VIII.B.1 imputes knowledge of officers "of the Policyholder". Whose knowledge or act counts can turn on the mismatch.

The definition makes the Policy Period subject to prior termination "in accordance with Section VII.C", but Section VII is the Notices section and the cancellation provision is Section VIII.C. The cross-reference is wrong on its face.

"Pollutants" is expanded by "shall also mean any other air emission, odor, ... noise, and electric, magnetic or electromagnetic field", a catch-all far broader than the hazardous-substance specifics it follows. Its reach in an employment-practices context is contestable.

"Potential Claim" is any "allegation or accusation" that does not constitute a Claim but "subsequently may give rise to a Claim", a boundary that depends on an unmeasured possibility of future assertion. Whether a given complaint was a Potential Claim or already a Claim is the sort of question the Awareness Provision forces.

"Retaliation" is "illegal retaliatory treatment of Employees, including" four enumerated activities, so it is unclear whether unlisted protected activity is within the definition. The word "including" against a specific list creates the usual scope question.

The definition qualifies subsidiary status by reference to entities "covered pursuant to Section VIII.A.1", but VIII.A.1 deems an entity a Subsidiary only if its headcount is under ten percent and separately gives ninety days' coverage to larger acquisitions. Reading the two together leaves the status of a mid-sized acquired entity unclear.

The definition reaches persons who are "or attempted to be" a customer or vendor, an undefined phrase, while excluding Claims by independent contractors. Whether a would-be customer qualifies would turn on "attempted to be".

Third Party Claims exclude Claims brought by independent contractors of the Policyholder, yet III.G and III.J treat certain independent contractors as Employees and Insured Individuals. The status of a contractor claimant depends on which definition controls.

The definition extends to acts by "any other persons for whom the Insureds are legally responsible", a catch-all whose reach beyond the Policyholder and Insured Individuals is undefined. Whether a given actor falls inside it is a question of construction.

"Wrongful demotion or adverse change in the terms, conditions or status of employment" is a general residual limb sitting after specific personnel actions, with no stated threshold of adversity. Its outer boundary would have to be construed.

The definition requires conduct that discriminates on listed grounds "or on any other basis prohibited by law", a catch-all appended to a closed list of protected characteristics. What other bases qualify is left open.

Exclusion A.5 lists eight statutes and then sweeps in "any other federal, state local or foreign statute or law similar to any statute or law described in (a) through (h)", a general catch-all against enumerated specifics whose reach is the classic ejusdem generis question. Exclusion A.2's "in any way involving" prior proceedings and Interrelated Wrongful Acts is equally open-textured.

Exclusion A.5(b) bars Claims for violation of laws governing employee benefit arrangements while Exclusion B.1 assumes Benefits claims are covered subject to a Defense-Costs-only limit, and A.3's collective-bargaining bar overlaps the carve-out in the definition of Claim. Reconciling the exclusions with those provisions requires construction.

The non-imputation sentence covers only Exclusion A.12(b) and only as between Insured Individuals, saying nothing about imputation to the Policyholder, which VIII.B.1 addresses on different terms. The interaction of the two imputation rules could be argued.

Exclusion B.4 ends with "or any other equitable remedy" after listing injunctive, declaratory and restitutionary relief, a catch-all of uncertain reach. Whether a particular monetary award is an "equitable remedy" would have to be construed.

Exclusion B.1 limits Benefits recovery to Defense Costs "provided that this Exclusion B.1 shall not apply to any Claim for wrongful termination", which sits against Exclusion A.5(b)'s outright bar on benefit-law claims. The two treat benefits-based losses differently.

The limit applies to "all Claims first made during the Policy Period", while Section II.C deems ERP Claims to be made in the preceding Policy Period and Section V.A's interrelated-claims rule relates Claims back to prior policies. Which Claims count against this limit depends on those deeming rules.

Exhaustion is said to extinguish all of the Insurer's obligations, while Section V.C imposes a duty to defend that ends only on exhaustion or rejection of a settlement; whether defense obligations for pending Claims survive is left to be reconciled. The two sentences address the same event from different directions.

The single-Claim rule aggregates all Claims arising from "the same Wrongful Act and/or all Interrelated Wrongful Acts" and back-dates them to the earliest of two events, using the elastic "Interrelated Wrongful Acts" definition. When a Claim is deemed first made is precisely what parties fight about under a claims-made policy.

The relation-back to "any prior policy" can push a Claim outside the Policy Period even though Insuring Agreement I and the Declarations notice promise coverage for Claims first made during the Policy Period. The interaction with Section II.C's ERP deeming compounds the problem.

The Retention applies to "a Claim", but Section V.A deems multiple related Claims to be one Claim and Item 4 states the Retention as "Each Claim"; how many retentions apply to a group of related suits is left to be worked out. The two provisions must be read together to answer it.

The Insurer has "both the right and the duty to defend" and to appoint counsel, yet the next paragraphs bar the Insureds from incurring any Defense Costs without consent and the hammer clause assumes the Insureds' consent is needed to settle. Who controls defense and settlement is not consistently allocated.

Defense ends "after the rejection of a settlement offer as described below", but the hammer clause below caps liability rather than describing any rejection that terminates the defense. The cross-reference does not match the provision it points to.

The consent requirement is qualified by "which shall not be unreasonably withheld", an unmeasured standard governing the Insureds' ability to settle or incur costs. Reasonableness of a withheld consent is a standard litigation question.

The bar on the Insureds incurring any Defense Costs without consent is hard to square with Section V.C's grant to the Insurer of the duty to defend and with the Insureds' right to associate at their own expense. Whether pre-tender or independent-counsel costs are recoverable depends on that fit.

The cooperation duty extends to "all information, assistance and cooperation that the Insurer reasonably requests", with no limit on subject-matter and reasonableness left undefined. Breach of that duty is asserted as a coverage defense and turns on the phrase.

"Shall not knowingly take any action which increases the Insurer's exposure for Loss" is open-ended: ordinary litigation and business decisions may increase exposure. What counts as a prohibited action cannot be bounded from the text.

The hammer clause turns on the Insureds "unreasonably refus[ing] to consent" to a settlement, an unmeasured standard with no mechanism for determining reasonableness. Whether the cap applies would be litigated on that word.

The clause presupposes that the Insureds' consent is required to settle, but Section V.C gives the Insurer the right and duty to defend and appoint counsel and nowhere else grants the Insureds a consent right. The settlement mechanics of the two paragraphs do not line up.

The provision hinges on an Insured "becom[ing] aware" of a Potential Claim and on a later Claim "arising from" it, neither of which is measured. Whether a subsequent suit arises from the noticed circumstances is the standard notice-of-circumstance fight.

Deeming a later Claim to have been made in the earlier Policy Period sits against Insuring Agreement I and the Declarations notice, which cover only Claims first made during the Policy Period or ERP. The relationship between the Awareness Provision and the claims-made condition requires construction.

The sentence denies coverage for fees incurred "prior to the time such circumstances result in a Claim", but "such circumstances" has no antecedent in the paragraph, which speaks of a Potential Claim. The referent must be supplied by construction.

The detailed notice contents are made a "condition precedent to exercising their rights hereunder", without saying whether substantial compliance suffices or whether omission of one listed item forfeits coverage. That is a live question wherever a circumstance notice is challenged.

This gives sixty days after the Claim is first made for a Claim resulting from a Potential Claim, while Insuring Agreement I requires reporting no later than sixty days after expiration of the Policy Period. The two outside dates conflict for a Claim made near or after expiry.

Notices "must" be delivered by prepaid express courier, certified mail or fax, an exclusive list that omits ordinary mail, hand delivery and e-mail. Whether notice given by an unlisted method is effective is the expressio unius question.

Notices must go to "the appropriate party" at the Item 11 address, and Item 11 lists two different fax numbers for claim notices and all other notices. Which address is "appropriate" for a given notice, and the effect of using the other, is left open.

Notice is deemed received on actual receipt or one day after sending, "whichever is earlier", so a notice is deemed received a day after dispatch even if it never arrives. The word "earlier" appears to invert the usual rule and changes the meaning of the clause.

An acquired entity is deemed a Subsidiary only if its headcount does not exceed ten percent of Employees, while the next paragraph gives ninety-day coverage where post-Transaction headcount exceeds one hundred and ten percent; the boundary case and the gap between the two tests are not addressed. The two paragraphs must be read together to know what an acquisition buys.

The clause reads "shall provide insurance for such entities ... as for a period of ninety (90) days", where the stray "as" leaves the scope of the ninety-day grant unclear. The sentence cannot be read as written without supplying words.

This ninety-day grant applies where headcount exceeds 110%, while the preceding paragraph deems entities Subsidiaries only under the 10% test; whether an entity can be both, or neither, is unresolved. The two coverage triggers overlap at the margin.

The paragraph begins mid-sentence without its conditional "if" or subparagraph label and reads "after such or acquisition", so its trigger has to be reconstructed. It also grants coverage only for "newly hired employees", a phrase not used elsewhere in the Policy.

This says coverage after a change of control "shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company", while Section VIII.C.1 gives the Parent Company an unqualified right to cancel during the Policy Period. The two provisions give opposite answers on the same facts.
Notice of a change of control is due "as soon as practicable" with no outside date and no stated consequence for late notice. The standard would have to be applied case by case.

The Insurer is said to have relied on statements in the Application and in the original application to a different insurer at the Continuity Date, which expands the rescission basis defined in III.A and sits against the severability rules in VIII.B.1 and B.2. The interaction determines whose misstatement voids whose coverage.

Making all Application statements "the basis of this Policy" and incorporating them sits against the Alteration and Assignment clause, which says the Policy alone constitutes the entire agreement between the Insureds and the Insurer. Whether extrinsic application materials are part of the contract turns on that pairing.

Only the knowledge of an enumerated list of officers is imputed to the Policyholder, an exclusive list whose treatment of functional equivalents and subsidiary officers is unaddressed. Whose knowledge counts is decided by that list.

Severability protects Insured Individuals from imputation, but VIII.B.1 imputes senior officers' knowledge to the Policyholder and IV.A.12 imputes nothing between Individuals; the combined effect on entity coverage is not spelled out. The provisions must be harmonised to know what can be rescinded.

The Parent Company's unqualified right to cancel conflicts with Section VIII.A.2, which provides that after a change of control coverage "shall not be cancellable by the Parent Company". A court would have to decide which governs.
Refunds on a Parent Company cancellation are "on the customary short rate basis", a trade term the Policy nowhere defines or quantifies. The size of the refund would turn on what is customary.

This paragraph is numbered "5" although the preceding nonrenewal-notice paragraph is also numbered 5, so cross-references to subsection 5 are ambiguous. The duplication is a mechanical defect on the face of the section.

The clause reads "prior of current" and makes the Policy excess only as to Loss from a Third Party Claim, leaving unclear how it operates where a single Claim mixes third-party and employment allegations. The garbled phrase and the narrow trigger both require reading in.

"[I]ntended to provide primary insurance" states an intention rather than an obligation and must be read against the preceding excess-only sentence for Third Party Claims. Whether it is operative could be argued.
The Insureds must "do everything necessary" to secure the Insurer's subrogation rights, an obligation without stated limit or cost allocation. What that requires of an insured is open.

Making "full compliance with all the terms of this Policy" a condition precedent to any action is absolute on its face, with no materiality or prejudice qualifier. Whether an immaterial breach bars suit is exactly the kind of question this wording generates.
The clause bars joinder in an action "to determine the Insureds' ability", where "ability" is plainly a mistake for "liability". As written the prohibition has no sensible referent.

The Parent Company acts for all Insureds on notices except notice electing the Extended Reporting Period, while Section II.C gives that election to "the Policyholder or the Insured Individuals"; who may elect and pay is left to be reconciled. The carve-out and the ERP clause do not clearly match.

The entire-agreement statement is difficult to square with Section VIII.B, which incorporates all Application statements into the Policy as its basis, and with III.A's expansive definition of Application. Whether extrinsic application materials form part of the contract turns on that conflict.

The clause says notice to or knowledge possessed by anyone "shall not effect a waiver of or estop" either party, purporting to bar waiver and estoppel entirely without carving out conduct-based waiver. Its reach against express conduct of the Insurer would have to be construed.
